articles.title: Meet Ava Grace Cummings, the 18-year-old North Carolina student who modelled STAC3 disorder, a rare hereditary muscle disease first identified in the Lumbee Tribe, in fruit flies and won $175,000 from Regeneron
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Ava Grace Cummings, an 18-year-old from North Carolina, wins $175,000 in the Regeneron Science Talent Search for her groundbreaking research on STAC3 disorder, a rare muscle disease in the Lumbee tribe, using fruit flies for potential new therapies.
articles.body: The Regeneron Science Talent Search is described by the Society for Science as the nation's oldest and most prestigious science and maths competition for high school seniors. It makes sense that most projects address issues that are somewhat unrelated to the researcher's personal life. Ava Grace Cummings made the opposite decision. The senior from Smithfield, North Carolina, who is eighteen years old, based her research on an illness she had personally witnessed in the faces of people she knew.Cummings, a member of the Lumbee and Coharie tribes, won second place and $175,000 in the 2025 competition for a study that used laboratory fruit flies to model STAC3 disorder, a rare genetic muscular condition. The flies were then used to test alternative therapies, including one based on traditional Indigenous herbal medicine.A sickness deeply ingrained in her own cultureFormerly known as Native American myopathy, STAC3 disorder is a congenital ailment that lowers muscle tone from birth and can cause joint stiffness, a cleft palate, a bent spine, and a potentially fatal reaction to some anaesthetic medications. It was initially identified in babies from the Lumbee tribe of North Carolina in the late 1980s, and it was subsequently linked to a single genetic mutation that was inherited among the group. GeneReviews estimates that STAC3 disorder affects about one in 5,000 Lumbee Native Americans. The condition has also been identified in other populations, including patients in southern Africa.For Cummings, STAC3 disorder was never an abstract condition. She told the Society for Science that seeing friends and family in the Lumbee Tribe struggle with the disease motivated her to raise awareness and look for potential treatments. There is no cure for STAC3 disorder, making the search for possible therapies an important part of her project.Turning fruit flies into a model of disease in actionTo study the rare muscle condition without human patients, Cummings turned to Drosophila. The fruit fly is widely used in genetics research because its short life cycle makes it possible to alter genes and observe changes over a relatively short period. Cummings created a strain of flies that did not express the dstac gene, the fly counterpart of the gene disrupted in STAC3 disorder. The resulting flies showed muscle-weakness traits that allowed her to model the condition in the laboratory.Armed with a workable model, she investigated two prospective therapies. One was Tirasemtiv, an experimental drug being studied for its effects on muscle contraction and neuromuscular function. The other was stinging nettle, Urtica dioica, a plant that many traditional herbal medicines employed, some of which her tribe used. She tested affected adult flies by measuring how well they climbed the walls of a test vial, while the larvae were assessed by the distance they travelled. Flies treated with nettle extract alone climbed better, while the larvae also travelled farther than untreated groups. The combination of nettle extract and Tirasemtiv produced the strongest improvement among the treatments tested.Connecting Two Medical SystemsRather than seeing Indigenous medicine and pharmaceutical research as two separate worlds, Cummings considers her study an attempt to bring the two into parity. She has said she hopes her study will bring greater attention, funding and therapeutic interest to illnesses that impact small, unique populations and are otherwise easily overlooked by the broader medical research system.During high school, she attended the North Carolina School of Science and Mathematics in Durham, where she founded and led the school's Natives Rising chapter. She also plays the piano, is a member of her school soccer team and serves as a resident life advisor. Cummings' second-place finish was also part of a notable milestone for the competition. Alongside fourth-place winner Logan Lee, a Native Hawaiian student, she was one of two Indigenous students to receive a top-10 prize in the 2025 Regeneron Science Talent Search. Native America Calling reported that it was the first time two Indigenous students had received top-10 awards in the competition's 83-year history.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Built in 1878, this 8,500-sq-ft Ohio jail held prisoners for 110 years; 148 years later, a developer bought it and may turn its cells into offices or a speakeasy
articles.summary: US News: A former Ohio jail that spent more than a century behind bars is getting a very different future. The historic Jail and Sheriff’s Residence in Delawar.
articles.body: A former Ohio jail that spent more than a century behind bars is getting a very different future. The historic Jail and Sheriff’s Residence in Delaware, Ohio, has been sold by the Delaware County Historical Society to Westwood principal Andy Warnock, a Delaware native, states the Columbus Business First report. The 8,500-square-foot property, which once housed prisoners and the county sheriff’s family, is now being repositioned as a mixed-use property that could include private offices, creative space and an unusual nod to its Prohibition-era past. The sale follows more than five years of stewardship by the Historical Society, which purchased the building in 2021 and worked to make it accessible through tours, exhibitions and community events, adds the report.A jail with more than 100 years of historyBuilt in 1878 by Toledo architect David Gibbs, the building operated as a working jail until 1988. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1990. Its architecture is primarily Italianate, with Gothic Revival and Second Empire influences that reflect the period in which it was built. The property also offers a glimpse into changing attitudes toward incarceration in 19th-century Ohio. The jail contains 18 cells, with 16 originally intended for men and two for women. The sheriff lived on the premises with his family, while the sheriff’s wife, known as the Matron, had responsibilities that included preparing meals and caring for inmates. The arrangement was part of a broader prison-reform movement associated with Ohio Governor Rutherford B. Hayes, who was born and raised in Delaware.From prison cells to private officesThe new plans are considerably more modern. Renovations to the property include HVAC and electrical improvements, along with updates to the rooms in the former residential section. Eight private offices are planned for that portion of the building, while shared amenities will include a kitchenette, conference room and lounge.Westwood Real Estate Co., the brokerage arm of Westwood Collective, plans to use part of the renovated space as it expands into the Delaware market and recruits residential and commercial real estate agents. Architects Dave Kerr and Cara Hering of DK Architects are working on the project.A speakeasy behind bars?Perhaps the most intriguing possibility involves the jail itself. The existing cells are expected to receive their own refresh during a second phase of renovation. Among the concepts being considered for the rear portion of the building are a Prohibition-era speakeasy and a maker’s space combined with an art gallery. It is a fittingly unconventional next act for a building that has already served as a jail, residence, museum and even wedding venue. In October 2025, the property hosted nine weddings during a Halloween-themed event organized by the City of Delaware and the Historical Society. Court employees dressed in costume while the entrance and cells were decorated for the occasion.Preserving the past while moving forwardFor Warnock, the project represents more than another real estate investment. As a Delaware native, he is bringing two decades of industry experience back to his hometown while taking on the challenge of giving one of its most recognizable buildings a useful new life. The goal now is to preserve the character that makes the old jail special while allowing the property to function in a very different era. If the plans come together, the building's cells may soon hold businesses, artists or late-night patrons rather than prisoners, an unusual transformation for a landmark that has witnessed nearly 150 years of Delaware history.Image Courtesy: istock and Columbus Business FirstCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In the 18th century, Prickly Pear Cactus was introduced to South Africa by European settlers as living fencing, but it spread across 900,000 hectares and became an agricultural nightmare
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover the fascinating history of prickly pear cactus in South Africa, its introduction by European settlers, and its transformation from a useful plant to an invasive agricultural pest before becoming a cultivated crop once again.
articles.body: Opuntia ficus-indica, also commonly known as prickly pear, reached South Africa with European settlers in the 18th century, and became particularly useful as food, fodder and a living barrier around properties. It spread through the country's dry eastern regions, and by the early 20th century the wild plant had become a major agricultural problem, with estimates putting the affected area at about 900,000 hectares.The cactus originated in Mexico and neighbouring parts of Mesoamerica, and had already travelled from the Americas to Europe after the Spanish conquest and subsequently moved through other parts of the world. A historical study by William Beinart and Luvuyo Wotshela records that O. ficus-indica, one of the most common prickly pears in South Africa, reached Graaff-Reinet with early white settlers in the 18th century. The plant initially spread because people found practical uses for it, which included fruit, fodder and hedging.A useful boundary plantPrickly pear could do something ordinary fencing could not, that is, it could grow in dry country while producing a dense barrier of spiny pads. A later review of southern African pasture and forage plants records that settlers carried O. ficus-indica into arid and semi-arid parts of the subcontinent, where it was cultivated as a living fence as well as for its fruit. The cactus also provided fodder during dry periods.Individual pads could establish new plants, while seeds were spread by animals and through the movement of people and livestock. Prickly pear found more disturbed ground and fewer barriers to its spread as cultivation and livestock farming expanded into the semi-arid interior.By the early 20th century, dense stands had formed across parts of the Eastern Cape and Karoo, and the plant could form thickets that restricted movement and reduced the amount of usable grazing land. The historical literature places the worst infestation at roughly 900,000 hectares, and a study of prickly pear in the Eastern Cape records that the plant was estimated to cover that area at its height in the 1930s, when agricultural officials and farmers increasingly treated the wild cactus as an invasive pest.South Africa turned to insectsMechanical removal was difficult because the cactus could occupy large areas and regenerate from surviving plant material, and South Africa therefore became an early testing ground for biological control. The government introduced insects that attacked prickly pear, including the cochineal insect Dactylopius opuntiae and the cactus moth Cactoblastis cactorum. The insects damaged the cactus itself rather than requiring workers to remove individual plants.Research published in Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment records the scale of the change. The authors found that the original 900,000-hectare infestation of O. ficus-indica had been reduced to less than 100,000 hectares by the time of their 1991 review, and the remaining populations were concentrated in cooler, wetter areas where the cochineal insect was less effective.The insects did not distinguish neatly between unwanted wild plants and cultivated varieties; as biological control reduced the invasive populations, it also affected cultivated cactus, which changed the role of prickly pear in South African agriculture. The wild, spiny forms were treated as invasive plants, while spineless cultivars remained useful for fruit and livestock feed.From weed to crop againThe ResearchGate-published Cactusnet briefing notes that about 1,500 hectares were being cultivated for fruit in South Africa, and another 3,000 hectares for fodder at the time of publication. Modern production relies mainly on spineless varieties that are managed as crops rather than allowed to spread freely.Prickly pear first entered South Africa as a useful plant, became an extensive agricultural pest, and was later brought under enough biological control for some forms to return to productive farming. Its earlier spread remains one of the better-known cases in South Africa of a plant introduced for practical use becoming difficult to contain across a large agricultural landscape.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In the 1870s, Russian Thistle was accidentally introduced to South Dakota by Russian immigrants, but it spread to 100 million acres and became the iconic tumbleweed
articles.summary: US News: Discover the fascinating history of Russian thistle, a plant that inadvertently became a significant invasive species in the US, transforming landscapes and agriculture since its introduction in the 1870s.
articles.body: Russian thistle first appeared in North America in the 1870s near Bon Homme County, South Dakota, after its seeds seemed to have arrived after mixing with flaxseed brought from the Russian Empire. The plant had spread across much of the American West within a few decades, and by 1910, it was estimated to occupy about 100 million acres of arid and semi-arid land. Today, the plant is better known as the tumbleweed.Salsola tragus is commonly called Russian thistle, and originated in dry parts of Europe and Central Asia. Its first known North American appearance was in South Dakota, where it found a landscape increasingly altered by farming. Farmers were clearing native prairie vegetation and repeatedly disturbing the soil to grow crops. Russian thistle was well suited to those conditions because it could establish where competing vegetation had been removed.The weed followed farms and railroadsIts seeds were similar in size to some cereal grains that made separating them mechanically difficult. Seeds could therefore remain mixed with agricultural shipments and move between farms, and threshing equipment also carried seeds from one field to another. Grain and other agricultural materials could travel hundreds of miles, while seeds could also move through irrigation canals and ditches.The Natural History Museum in London describes Russian thistle as one of the fastest plant invasions in US history. By the beginning of the 20th century, it had reached California, where disturbed landscapes that were created by agriculture and overgrazing gave it additional territory. Its spread also coincided with a period when large areas of the Great Plains were being transformed for agriculture. Loose soil, reduced competition from native grasses and dry conditions created an environment in which Russian thistle could establish quickly, and by the time farmers understood the scale of the invasion, the plant was no longer confined to the place where it had first appeared.A plant built to rollThe plant begins as a relatively soft seedling, but it develops stiff and spiny branches as it matures. Eventually, the plant dries out and breaks away from its root, while its rounded structure allows wind to push it across open ground. Thousands of seeds can shake loose as the dead plant rolls, and the seeds may then remain dormant until conditions become suitable for germination.The Natural History Museum says an individual plant can produce as many as 250,000 seeds, depending on its size. Russian thistle can also tolerate low moisture and alkaline or saline soils, which gives it an advantage in the dry environments where a lot of the invasion occurred. Dense infestations could interfere with ploughing, compete with crops and restrict grazing, while dry tumbleweeds also created a fire hazard as they accumulated against fences, buildings and other structures.About 100 million acresThe USDA Agricultural Research Service has described Russian thistle as an invasive alien weed that occupies about 100 million acres in the western United States. Its documented effects include infestations of fallow fields, blocked irrigation systems, traffic hazards and increased wildfire risk. In 2025, the USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service described Russian thistle as an alien annual weed that was infesting about 41.3 million hectares, which is equivalent to 100 million acres, across the western United States. The agency was evaluating the use of the blister mite Aceria salsolae as a biological-control agent to reduce infestations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: GURGAON: A friend of a woman biker chased down and confronted a car driver at a traffic signal after the vehicle hit her motorcycle on Gurgaon’s Golf Course Road, knocking her off the bike and dragging it for several metres.The incident took place on Sunday when the biker, Sia, was riding her Aprilia RS 457 sports bike with a group of bikers.She sustained injuries after falling onto the road, while the occupants of the car allegedly fled the spot following the collision.According to Sia, one of her friends pursued the car after the incident and managed to catch up with it at a traffic signal.The friend confronted the driver and allegedly told him that he was responsible for hitting Sia and asked him to stop.However, the driver allegedly denied responsibility and fled from the traffic signal, Sia claimed.The entire incident was captured on an action camera fitted to Sia’s motorcycle. She later shared the footage and details of the incident on her Instagram profile.Sia alleged that the car occupants had been following her from the beginning of the ride and appeared to be intoxicated. She said she asked them to maintain a safe distance, but they allegedly asked her to stop.She continued riding ahead to prevent the car from cutting her off, while a friend riding behind her tried to intervene by positioning his motorcycle to prevent the car from repeatedly coming alongside her.Despite this, Sia alleged, the car continued following her. She claimed that at one point, the driver attempted to cut across the path of her motorcycle, resulting in the collision.The impact knocked Sia off her bike, while the motorcycle was dragged several metres along the road. The car then allegedly fled the area.Sia has appealed to Gurgaon Police to investigate the incident and take action against the driver. articles.title: In the early 1800s, Giant Hogweed was introduced by British explorers for ornamental gardens, but it spread beyond control and is now a feared invasive plant
articles.summary: UK News: Discover the invasive threat of giant hogweed, a once-desired ornamental plant that now poses ecological and health risks. Learn about its history and management challenges.
articles.body: Giant hogweed can rise several metres above surrounding vegetation, producing enormous leaves and broad clusters of white flowers. But Heracleum mantegazzianum is now regarded very differently from the ornamental curiosity that was once welcomed into European gardens.According to Plants of the World Online, giant hogweed (Heracleum mantegazzianum) is native to the Caucasus but has been introduced to parts of Europe and other regions outside its natural range. In Britain, it escaped from cultivation and became established in parts of the countryside, particularly along waterways, where its large size, abundant seed production and vigorous growth have made it a challenging invasive species to manage.From botanical curiosity to wild plantThe story began with plant collectors and horticultural experts bringing rare species to Britain and continental Europe. Historical records from the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, show that giant hogweed was listed there in 1817, appearing in a seed list. By 1828, a naturalised population had been recorded in Cambridgeshire. The plant was introduced to Britain mainly as an ornamental species, with its unusual height and imposing appearance making it attractive to gardeners and collectors. This means the often-repeated claim that giant hogweed was brought to Britain by British explorers in the early 1800s needs some qualification. Historical evidence instead points to a wider network of botanical gardens, plant collectors and estates exchanging seeds and cultivating plants that had been introduced from the Caucasus.Once outside cultivated gardens, however, the plant had characteristics that helped it establish itself. Research published in the Journal of Applied Ecology found that giant hogweed and other large invasive plants could become widespread after escaping cultivation, particularly along watercourses. Their rapid growth and large size allow them to dominate local vegetation, while their presence can reduce the conservation value of invaded sites.A plant built for spreadingThe success of giant hogweed may be partially attributed to the sheer number of seeds that can be produced by each plant. A single plant can produce thousands of seeds, which may travel short distances by wind and farther via rivers and other waterways. The plant can also overwhelm smaller vegetation. It can form large stands, shading plants beneath its leaves and competing for space and resources. When the stems die back, bare ground may be left exposed, potentially contributing to erosion along riverbanks during high water flow. These traits contributed to giant hogweed becoming recognised as an ecological problemResearch published in the Journal of Environmental Management has examined the management of invasive giant hogweed and the difficulties involved in controlling established populations. The research highlights how management needs to consider the plant's biology and the persistence of populations rather than relying on simply removing visible mature plants.The plant is not limited to Britain. According to the Plants of the World Online database at Kew, Heracleum mantegazzianum is indigenous to the Caucasus region, but is naturalised to a wide variety of nations in Europe, North America, and New Zealand. Its attractive qualities helped the species spread through several channels and become established in other regions.The plant also poses a health riskGiant hogweed gained notoriety because it poses a danger not only to native flora. The sap contains furanocoumarins that cause photosensitivity in human skin. Skin contact combined with sun exposure may lead to photodermatitis, which is characterised by burning, blistering and discolouration. Some consequences can be long-term. This health risk led to a different approach to the plant. In Britain, giant hogweed is included in the list of non-native invasive plants according to Schedule 9 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act.People should avoid touching giant hogweed with exposed skin, and the Royal Horticultural Society recommends professional removal for garden infestations. Its ecological invasiveness and health risks make it far more than an ordinary gardening task. Giant hogweed’s history began in a fairly ordinary way. The plant found its way to Britain as a desired ornamental species. More than 200 years later, the plant is viewed as one that should not be intentionally grown or dispersed. The story shows how introducing a new exotic plant into a garden can have consequences far bigger than expected.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Took 80 years to restore full glory of Vande Mataram': Amit Shah
articles.summary: India News: Union home minister Amit Shah on Monday said it took nearly 80 years to restore the “full glory” of the national song Vande Mataram, underlining its e.
articles.body: Union home minister Amit Shah on Monday said it took nearly 80 years to restore the “full glory” of the national song Vande Mataram, underlining its enduring role in India's cultural and national identity.Addressing the 6th All India Rajbhasha Sammelan, Shah said the song had played an important role in India’s freedom struggle and remained deeply connected with the country’s cultural consciousness.Shah also linked the promotion of Indian languages with what he described as cultural nationalism, saying the objective was to create greater awareness about India's rich culture and history.“Cultural nationalism means creating awareness about our culture and history,” Shah said, stressing that linguistic diversity should be seen as a strength rather than a source of division.Shah defends NEPThe Union home minister also defended the provision in the National Education Policy (NEP) encouraging students to learn another Indian language apart from their mother tongue.He said those opposing the provision were committing a “sin”.Shah said the policy was aimed at strengthening familiarity among Indians with each other’s languages and cultures, rather than imposing any particular language.He also highlighted Maharashtra’s linguistic diversity, describing it as the country’s only multi-linguistic state. Shah noted that Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government had accorded Classical Language status to Marathi, recognising its rich literary and historical heritage."It was none other than our PM Modi who took the initiative to grant Marathi the status of a 'Classical Language.' When you step onto the soil of Maharashtra, you find a place where diverse languages, such as Konkani, Gujarati, Sindhi, Hindi, Kannada, and Warli that have flourished, been respected, and gained acceptance. There is no multilingual state in all of India larger than Maharashtra; if there is a state that stands out as the largest multilingual region, it is Maharashtra," he said.The home minister further said the NEP had placed considerable emphasis on education in Indian languages. He said PM Modi had made imparting primary education in the mother tongue mandatory under the new education policy.Shah's remarks came amid a broader push by the government to promote Indian languages in education and public administration, while emphasising the cultural links between language, history and national identity.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: India to supply 654MW of electricity for 18 hours daily to Nepal after deadly floods cripple power sector
articles.summary: India News: India has approved the export of up to 654 MW of electricity to Nepal for 18 hours a day until December 31, following devastating floods that damaged .
articles.body: India has approved the export of up to 654 MW of electricity to Nepal for 18 hours a day until December 31, following devastating floods that damaged hydropower infrastructure and sharply reduced the Himalayan nation's domestic generation capacity, the Ministry of Power said on Monday.The approval, effective from September 13, allows electricity exports to the Nepal Electricity Authority between midnight and 6 pm, according to the ministry.Up to 600 MW will be supplied through the Muzaffarpur-Dhalkebar 400 kV double-circuit line, while another 54 MW can be transmitted through the Tanakpur-Mahendranagar 132 kV single-circuit line, the ministry said."The recent floods in Nepal have caused significant damage to hydropower infrastructure, reducing the country's domestic power generation capacity and creating an additional requirement for electricity," the Ministry of Power said in a release."The approval will help Nepal meet its power requirements during this difficult period and further strengthen the close and longstanding energy cooperation between India and Nepal," it added.The ministry said the quantum of electricity to be exported from January 2027 would be reviewed in December 2026. "The quantum of power to be exported from January 2027 will be reviewed in December 2026," it said.The floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated parts of northern and central Nepal. According to Nepal's national disaster risk rreduction and management authority, the death toll had reached 1,385, while 5,130 people remained missing as of September 11. More than 12 hydropower plants were reportedly swept away or damaged.About 900 power station workers are among those reported missing, further affecting the country's electricity generation capacity. Nepal, where hydropower supplies almost all electricity, had also halted power exports and said it would buy electricity from India to meet domestic requirements.India has separately continued its relief and rescue support. The ministry of external affairs said eight special flights since August 26 had delivered more than 130 tonnes of relief material, while 54 expert personnel had been deployed for rescue, relief and forensic operations."The assistance includes standard relief supplies such as temporary shelters, blankets, hygiene kits, solar lamps and medicines," the MEA said, besides specialised equipment for tunnel and mud rescue operations and DNA profiling.The United States has also approved $1 million to strengthen Nepal Police's DNA and forensic identification capacity. The US State Department said the latest assistance takes Washington's humanitarian, health and forensic support following the floods to more than $5 million.Nepal has meanwhile sought China's assistance to rebuild the Syaphrubesi-Rasuwagadhi road, a key trade route that was severely damaged. Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal told The Kathmandu Post that "China has given us a verbal commitment to provide assistance, although a written agreement has not yet been signed."Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: The US wants to swap federal land on Georgia’s Cumberland Island for privately owned parcels; any parkland leaving federal ownership would be permanently barred from subdivision and major development
articles.summary: US News: An unusual land-swap proposal on a remote Georgia barrier island is putting a new twist on the question of what happens when private property and prot.
articles.body: An unusual land-swap proposal on a remote Georgia barrier island is putting a new twist on the question of what happens when private property and protected public land overlap. The US National Park Service (NPS) is considering two voluntary land exchanges at Cumberland Island National Seashore, under which it would acquire privately owned parcels in environmentally sensitive parts of the island while transferring federal land to private landowners in return.But there is an important catch: land leaving federal ownership would remain under permanent conservation restrictions. The proposed conservation easements would prohibit subdivision and permanently limit development, meaning the land could become privately owned without simply becoming open for unrestricted construction.The NPS opened a 30-day public comment period on September 9, with comments being accepted until October 16, 2026. The agency says the environmental assessment examines the potential effects of the exchanges on Cumberland Island’s natural, cultural and human environment.Why is the NPS considering a land swap?Cumberland Island is not made up entirely of federally owned land, despite being a national seashore. Private properties exist within the park boundary, creating a patchwork of ownership across an island otherwise known for its relatively undeveloped landscape. The proposed exchanges are intended to consolidate ownership in areas where private parcels currently intersect important park infrastructure and natural resources.Earlier NPS planning documents said some privately owned parcels intersect the island’s main road, important visitor-use areas and trails, as well as areas containing natural and cultural resources that the park wants to protect. Bringing these properties under NPS ownership could create more continuous corridors of publicly managed land and make long-term management easier.A March 2026 presentation to Camden County described the proposed acquisition as covering approximately 142 acres. It said the exchange could help protect live-oak maritime forests, beaches, potential historic and archaeological resources, the barrier-island ecosystem, shorebird nesting areas and habitat used by threatened sea turtles.The arrangement also addresses a practical problem: private ownership currently cuts across portions of the park’s road and trail systems. The proposed exchanges could reduce the need for separate rights-of-way and access agreements for those routes.What would happen to the federal land?This is where the proposal becomes particularly unusual. Instead of simply selling federal property, the NPS plans to transfer land subject to conservation easements. These legal restrictions would stay attached to the property even if ownership changes in the future.According to the NPS, the easements would permanently limit development, prohibit subdivision and provide protections for natural and cultural resources. The restrictions are intended to remain in place across future changes in ownership. That means federal ownership could change without removing the land entirely from the island’s conservation framework.The proposal has nevertheless attracted scrutiny because the land exchanged would become privately owned, even if significant restrictions remain. Reporting by The Current in June said draft agreements contemplated transferring roughly 20 acres of NPS land in one exchange and about 60 acres in another. The agreements also outlined the possibility of single-family residences on some of the transferred property, with proposed limits of up to 15,000 square feet per residence and a maximum height of 35 feet.Those details have become part of the debate over whether the proposed exchanges represent a sensible consolidation of protected land or could introduce new development pressure into a landscape prized for its undeveloped character.Cumberland Island is more than a beachThe island, off the coast of southeastern Georgia, is the state's largest barrier island and contains a mixture of maritime forest, salt marshes and beaches. More than 9,800 acres are designated wilderness, according to the NPS. Its isolation has helped preserve an unusual coastal ecosystem. The island provides habitat for a range of wildlife, including shorebirds and sea turtles, while its forests and marshes form part of a larger barrier-island system. That ecological character is one reason the ownership pattern matters.For park managers, a privately owned parcel embedded within or beside protected land can complicate everything from trail management to habitat protection. Acquiring strategically located private property could allow the NPS to manage a larger, more connected landscape. At the same time, transferring federal land to private owners raises a different question: how much public land should be exchanged to achieve that goal?Why the public is being asked to weigh inThe latest step is not a final approval of the land exchanges. The NPS is currently seeking public feedback as part of the environmental assessment process.The agency has described the transactions as voluntary and says it has worked with participating landowners to ensure that permanent conservation easements would accompany any federal land leaving government ownership. Superintendent Melissa Trenchik said the goal is to protect sensitive habitats, preserve the island's wilderness character and improve long-term stewardship.The issue has already generated opposition from some conservation groups. The Coalition to Protect America's National Parks and other organizations requested a formal public hearing after the environmental assessment was released, arguing that the proposed exchanges warrant greater public scrutiny.The debate therefore goes beyond a simple question of public versus private ownership. The NPS says the swaps could bring ecologically important private parcels into public ownership and create a more manageable landscape. Critics are questioning what the government would give up in return and what private development could eventually occur on the transferred land despite the conservation restrictions.The NPS is accepting public comments through October 16. A public meeting is scheduled for September 23 in St. Marys, Georgia, where agency officials are expected to explain the environmental assessment and answer questions about the proposed transactions.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Goa club fire: Accused Luthra brothers surrender after SC rejects bail relief, sent to judicial custody
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Birch by Romeo Lane nightclub owners Saurabh and Gaurav Luthra, along with their business partner Ajay Gupta, surrendered before a Goa cour.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Birch by Romeo Lane nightclub owners Saurabh and Gaurav Luthra, along with their business partner Ajay Gupta, surrendered before a Goa court on Monday. Two weeks after the Supreme Court refused to interfere with the cancellation of their bail, the accused surrendered in the case over the December 2025 fire that killed 25 people.They turned themselves in before the Mapusa additional district and sessions court after the Supreme Court directed them to surrender within two weeks. Advocate Saumya Drago, who represents the accused, said the court accepted their surrender and issued the necessary remand orders.Drago also said the defence filed an application seeking medical accommodations for the three men based on their medical history, doctors' prescriptions and medical records. The court allowed their requests for medicines and a mattress but kept the request for special footwear pending. It sought a response from the investigating officer, with the matter expected to be taken up on the next working day, she said.The Supreme Court had on August 31 dismissed the accused's petitions challenging the Bombay high court's decision to cancel their bail. It also directed the trial court to expedite the proceedings.The Bombay high court had cancelled the trio's bail on August 18, citing the seriousness of the case and the need for further legal proceedings. The accused then moved the Supreme Court against the order.The fire broke out at the Birch by Romeo Lane nightclub in Arpora, North Goa, on December 6, 2025. It killed 25 people and injured several others.The chargesheet filed in the case accuses the three men of offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, including culpable homicide not amounting to murder, acts endangering human life, negligent conduct with respect to fire and combustible matter, forgery, using forged documents as genuine and criminal conspiracy.The chargesheet alleged that "irresponsible acts" of the accused resulted in the deaths of 25 people in the mass-casualty incident, causing "irreparable loss" to their families.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Suspected spy accused of giving info to Russian intelligence in Berlin
articles.summary: German prosecutors have filed charges against a suspected spy for Russia, accusing her of passing information to an intelligence operative at the Russian emb...
articles.body:
German prosecutors have charged a suspected spy for Russia with covert intelligence agent activity, accusing her of passing information to an intelligence operative at the Russian embassy.

The German-Ukrainian dual national, who has been in custody since January, allegedly provided the intelligence officer with tips about high-profile events and tried to recruit individuals from the Ministry of Defence and arms industry for her purposes.

The suspect, who has been in contact with the intelligence officer since at least October 2023, sought information on German defence policy and the arms industry in relation to Russia's war on Ukraine, with the courts now tasked with deciding whether the case should proceed to trial.

German prosecutors have filed charges against a suspected spy for Russia, accusing her of passing information to an intelligence operative at the Russian embassy.

Federal prosecutors based in Karlsruhe said on Monday she had been charged with covert intelligence agent activity.

The German-Ukrainian dual national was arrested in January and has been in custody since then.

The alleged agent is said to have been in contact with the intelligence officer since October 2023 at the latest.

"For years, the accused provided him with numerous tips about high-profile events and ensured that he was able to attend such events, in some cases under a false name," the prosecutors' statement said.

"This was intended to enable him to build his own network for intelligence purposes."

The suspect also tried to "recruit people from the Ministry of Defence and from the arms industry for her purposes," the prosecutors said.

Acting on behalf of the intelligence officer, she sought information on German defence policy and the arms industry, particularly in relation to Russia's war on Ukraine.

The courts must now decide whether the case should go to trial.

articles.title: 'Protect our children online': Macron urges EU to fast-track social media ban for kids under 15
articles.summary: Europe News: French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday reiterated his commitment to protecting children online and called on the European Union to quickly harmoni.
articles.body: French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday reiterated his commitment to protecting children online and called on the European Union to quickly harmonise a ban on social media use for children under 15.“From the very first day, I made a commitment: to protect our children online. We will see it through to the end,” Macron said in a post on X.Macron said France had completed technical work to revise the wording of its proposed ban following observations made by the Constitutional Council in mid-August. The government has now notified the European Commission of the revised proposal, he said.“Following the decision handed down by the Constitutional Council in mid-August on the ban of social networks for those under 15, I had tasked the Prime Minister with finding a path forward that complies with the Council's observations and European law. That has now been achieved,” Macron said.“After rigorous technical work, the Government is today notifying the Commission of new wording, one month after the Council's decision. This protection must also become the standard for all European children,” he added.Macron said he had conveyed to the president of the European Commission his determination to introduce the age restriction across the bloc and regulate platform features.“That is why I have shared with the President of the European Commission my determination that Europe move forward quickly and rigorously, to harmonize this ban at the Union level and regulate the features of platforms,” he said.He also thanked European Commission officials, parliamentarians and countries supporting the proposal.“Thanks to the determination of the President of the Commission, parliamentarians, and the support of many European states that share this exigency with us, I am pleased that the protection of minors online is now a priority for our Europe, at the heart of this back-to-school agenda,” Macron said.“France will provide its full support, with rigor and determination. Don't let up,” he added.France’s parliament voted in July to ban social media use for children under 15. Macron had then said the measure would take effect at the start of the school year, subject to review by the Constitutional Council.The move made France the first European Union country to introduce such an age limit, according to CNN. Other countries have also been considering restrictions on children’s access to social media. The United Kingdom announced plans in June to ban social media use for children under 16, ANI reported.Then Prime Minister Keir Starmer said excessive social media use could affect children’s sleep, playtime, family time and mental health.In Japan, a government panel proposed stricter age-verification requirements and greater responsibility for social media operators. Australia introduced a blanket social media ban for children under 16 last year, while Spain and Denmark have also been considering similar measures.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: UP assembly elections and fight for Muslim votes: Decoding SP, Congress's Owaisi problem
articles.summary: India News: That was Asaduddin Owaisi's outreach-cum-warning to Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav in July at a rally in Moradabad while he launched AIMIM’s cam.
articles.body: "I am ready to join hands. I am ready to form an alliance. Today is the time to talk. Don't cry later after the elections are over. We don't want the BJP to come to power again.”That was Asaduddin Owaisi's outreach-cum-warning to Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav in July at a rally in Moradabad while he launched AIMIM’s campaign for the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections due early next year.Seeking alliance with opposition parties is now a part of Owaisi’s playbook to counter allegations of being a vote-cutter and the B-team of the BJP. We have seen AIMIM adopt similar strategy in other states like Maharashtra and Bihar. In both these states, it went all out to seek space in larger opposition alliances before deciding to contest on its own when its offer was rejected. Then the "rejection: became a part of Owaisi's campaign: we asked you to come in, you kept us out, so don't blame us for what happens next."So, when Owaisi reached out to Samajwadi Party in July, it was on expected lines and did not come as a surprise. But there is now a twist in the tale.Owaisi’s Uttar Pradesh plans suffered a jolt this month when one of his most trusted aides and the party’s national spokesperson Syed Asim Waqar dumped the party to join the Congress.Waqar, who rose to prominence defending the AIMIM and its politics, was a prominent voice for AIMIM in Uttar Pradesh and hence his crossing over to the Congress potentially impacts Owaisi's bid to make electoral inroads in UP.But more than his exit, it was his parting remarks that will bother Owaisi. “Being in the AIMIM for so many years, I felt that we pay lip service by stating that the BJP must be removed, but on the ground, we don't fight the BJP; we fight the Congress, the SP; we are fighting every other person who wants to remove the BJP,” Waqar said when asked about his decision to leave the AIMIM.Justifying his switch, Waqar said, “If we (AIMIM) keep fighting the opposition and do not allow it to blossom, then we are helping the BJP. I have decided that if we are true nationalists and want to remove the BJP honestly, then our objective should be to fight the BJP. If we are fighting the enemies of the BJP, then we are friends of the BJP. In reality, if someone is fighting the BJP across the country, it is Congress, Rahul Gandhi and his team."Now, this is precisely the point which the opposition parties make against Owaisi and his AIMIM.AIMIM’s UP plansUttar Pradesh has been a difficult story for Owaisi. His AIMIM failed to win a single seat in the 2022 assembly elections in the state. And that makes the 2027 challenge a real test of whether the Bihar formula will work or whether Akhilesh is right to believe that AIMIM is a rival he can afford to ignore.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();Even while offering to join hands with Akhilesh, Owaisi chose to kick off AIMIM's 2027 campaign from Matera in Bahraich, a seat held by the Samajwadi Party. He also announced AIMIM’s candidate from the seat making his intent very clear.Owaisi questioned what SP leaders had done for the area despite getting Muslim votes, while saying AIMIM was ready for an alliance only if it was treated with 'respect' and given 'equal status'.The party has dropped enough signals to suggest that it is preparing for a much bigger push in UP in 2027. The party has also divided the state into zones and appointed regional in-charges as part of its attempt to strengthen the organisation before the election.AIMIM accepted that its performance was not up to the mark in 2022 but asserted that the party has spent the last few years trying to correct that.AIMIM's Uttar Pradesh president Shaukat Ali has said the party could contest around 200 seats if it fights alone. He has also kept the door open for a possible understanding with the BSP."Our natural alliance, if we were to forge one, would be with the BSP. Muslims and Dalits together account for nearly 40% of the vote share, enough to defeat both the SP and BJP," Ali said.The Samajwadi Party and the Congress will keep a close watch on AIMIM’s BSP outreach as it can have the potential to disrupt a lot of political calculations in the state. However, for now Mayawati has made it clear that her BSP will not forge any alliances with any party for elections.What makes UP challenge both interesting and difficultThe 2027 assembly elections in UP is likely to see a very keen contest for Muslim votes. The switching of sides by Asim Waqar exposes the keen contest among the non-BJP parties for support of Muslims in the upcoming elections.The Congress, which would consider this AIMIM import as a big boost to its prospects, had contested the 2024 Lok Sabha elections in alliance with the Samajwadi Party, and, as of now, they are both part of INDIA bloc ahead of next year’s assembly elections.But this alliance has not stopped the two parties from taking measures to consolidate their individual support bases. Last month, the Samajwadi Party got a boost when the son-in-law of Congress MP from UP’s Saharanpur Imran Masood joined the party in the presence of Akhilesh Yadav. Imran Masood has been very vocal against SP and its chief Akhilesh Yadav accusing them of imposing as the ‘big-brother’ in SP-Congress alliance for the 2027 UP polls.For the SP, the Alpsankhyaks (read Muslims) form an important component of Akhilesh Yadav’s PDA outreach. In fact, his success in Uttar Pradesh till now has been largely powered by the Yadavs and the Muslims. And while, Akhilesh desperately tries to broaden his support base by reaching out to the Dalits, women and even the Pandits, he cannot make big gains without the support of Muslims.However, that does not stop the Congress from making its own outreach to the community in a bid to try and win them back. After all, for several decades the Muslims had contributed to the electoral success of the Congress. It was only with the rise of regional parties that they drifted away from the grand-old-party. So, it will naturally be happy with Asim Waqar on its side.The AIMIM, which is the third pole of Muslim politics in the state, will try to take advantage of the posturing and war of words between the two alliance partners as it tries to find its space in the state.AIMIM has shown that it can become a serious player where its support is concentrated. What it has not yet shown is that it can do the same in Uttar Pradesh, where the Samajwadi Party remains the main beneficiary of Muslim votes against the BJP.Where AIMIM matters and where it doesn'tIn the 2023 Telangana assembly election, the party contested nine seats and won seven, underlining how strong its hold remains in parts of the state.Bihar has been its most successful experiment outside Telangana till now. The party managed to win five seats in 2020 and repeated the number in 2025, mainly in the Seemanchal region.In Maharashtra, AIMIM has pockets of support but won just one assembly seat in 2024. In Uttar Pradesh, the challenge has been tougher. In the 2022 assembly election, AIMIM contested 96 seats but failed to win any. Its statewide vote share remained below 1%.AIMIM’s Rajasthan experimentOwaisi’s move to contest the Panchayat and Municipal body elections in Rajasthan shows the party’s intent to expand its base in states where it was not a player till now. The AIMIM chief maintains that the state needs a strong third political alternative apart from the ruling BJP and the Congress which have been the dominant players in state’s politics till now.In a bid to disturb the duoploy, Owaisi has announced that if Rashtriya Loktantrik Party chief Hanuman Beniwal emerges as a third force, the AIMIM will support him and work together to challenge both major political parties.Owaisi said, “Hanuman Beniwal and AIMIM together will make the lives of BJP and Congress leaders difficult.” He also appealed to voters to support AIMIM candidates and RLP candidates contesting elections on the party’s bottle symbol.The BJP would be smiling either wayWhile the Congress and the other opposition parties keep an eye on AIMIM’s political moves, the BJP perhaps would not be worried much.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();When Owaisi had reached out to Akhilesh, BJP wasted no time in mocking the proposal. Former BJP spokesperson Shehzad Poonawalla had then called it a 'friend request' to Akhilesh and accused both parties of vote-bank politics.Akhilesh Yadav and Owaisi have long competed in appeasement politics. Now they have set aside the contest over who will be the bigger 'bhaijaan' and are looking at a 'bhaijaan collaboration'. Owaisi is effectively sending Akhilesh ji a friend request. They are two sides of the same coinFor the BJP, Owaisi can be useful either way, more so in Uttar Pradesh.If AIMIM contests separately and takes away even a small number of votes from SP-Congress in close seats, the BJP may benefit. If AIMIM joins the alliance, the BJP can use Owaisi's presence to sharpen its attack on the opposition over minority appeasement.Catch-22 for opposition partiesThe opposition parties are reluctant to accept Owaisi’s offer to ensure that non-BJP votes, especially of the Muslims, do not split. They know that Owaisi’s offer is like a double-edged sword.Most of these opposition parties like the RJD in Bihar, Samajwadi Party in Uttar Pradesh have banked heavily on the support of Muslims for their politics. If they accept AIMIM as an ally, they fear that Muslims will back Owaisi and gradually this will weaken their own minorities’ politics.Second, any opposition alliance with AIMIM will give the BJP a very strong weapon to engineer reverse polarisation. Since Owaisi is known for a very aggressive hardline brand of politics on issues concerning the minorities, the opposition will find it difficult to dissociate itself from the AIMIM. And this will give the BJP an opportunity to mobilise the Hindus against the opposition parties and eventually corner them.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Why the Houthi advance towards Yemen’s Marib, Taiz matters
articles.summary: Marib is home to Yemen’s oil sector. Whoever controls it secures economic gains. Taiz’s location makes it critical.
articles.body:
Yemen's government forces are engaging in air attacks against the Iran-backed Houthis to prevent their advances in Marib, the government's last stronghold in the north and a key oil and gas hub.

Heated battles are also taking place in western Taiz, where government forces, supported by Saudi Arabia, are on the counteroffensive after losing ground last week, with the strategic importance of Taiz lying in its geography as a bridge between the Houthi-held north and government-held south.

The Houthis' capture of Marib would be a significant turning point in the conflict, potentially granting them leverage in future negotiations and control over crucial energy infrastructure, while their advances towards the Bab al-Mandeb strait pose a threat to global trade and Saudi Arabia's oil exports.

Yemen's government forces have carried out air attacks against the Iran-backed Houthis to repel their advances, as the rebel group has been gaining ground in government-held positions in the past week.

The focus of the fighting is now shifting to the region of Marib – the government's last remaining stronghold in the north and a major oil and gas hub. Should the Houthis gain control of it, it could decisively turn the tide of the war in their favour, say analysts.

Heated battles are also taking place in western Taiz, on the western coast, where reports suggest government forces, supported by Saudi Arabia, are now on the counteroffensive after losing some ground there last week. A video released on Monday by the Yemeni army purports to show Houthi positions and vehicles being bombed there.

Trapped in the middle are the civilians. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) has reported that more than 85,000 have been forced to flee their homes since the beginning of September. More than 2,000 have fled into Djibouti's northern shores.

It is the last remaining stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in northern Yemen. A Houthi expansion there would threaten government presence and weaken its leverage in the north.

Marib also hosts the country's largest gas and oil fields, meaning that whoever controls it holds some of Yemen's most important energy infrastructure and a potentially crucial source of revenue.

"Dominating Marib's oil and gas resources has been a Houthi goal for more than a decade. Without facing a crushing defeat in Marib, they would keep fighting to achieve that goal," Saddam al-Huraibi, a Yemeni political commentator, told Al Jazeera . Should they gain control of it, the group could earn great leverage to negotiate favourable terms in any future mediation effort.

A Houthi capture of Marib would be a "watershed moment" in terms of the country's internal dynamics, said Adam Baron, a fellow at the Future Security Program of the New America think tank. Still, he said, it will be a tough fight as government forces will see this battle as an existential war. "Losing Marib would be an absolute crushing defeat" for the forces of Yemen's internationally recognised government, he added.

Marib is also geographically significant because it lies on the easiest road that runs from northern Yemen to Shabwa Governorate in the south – a seafront on the Gulf of Aden and the Arabian Sea – and al-Mahra Governorate.

The optics of a win in Marib would also be a powerful propaganda tool for the Houthis, helping them convince many Yemenis that the group is on a roll militarily and is poised for even greater victories, said Nabil Hetari, a Yemeni writer and human rights activist.

There is also a humanitarian dimension. Over the years, the city has been welcoming displaced people from areas which have fallen under Houthi control since the fall of the capital Sanaa in 2014. According to IOM figures from 2023, Yemen recorded nearly 2.8 million internally displaced people, more than half of whom (58 percent) are in Marib.

"All the parties involved in the battle are focused on Marib as a potential decider in the nature of their exit from this war," said Hetari.

The strategic importance of Taiz lies in its geography.

The governorate forms a bridge between the Houthi-held north and the government-held south and the Red Sea coast. Thus, whoever controls it gains the upper hand in the movement of weapons and supplies between the interior and the southern port city of Aden.

Taiz also carries considerable political weight. One of Yemen's largest population centres, the city became an important centre of resistance to the Houthis after they seized Sanaa in 2014 and has endured years of fighting and restrictions on access. A major Houthi breakthrough there would therefore carry symbolic significance far beyond the territory captured.

Its western coast also stretches towards Mocha, a historic town that the Houthis captured last week, and towards the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a chokepoint connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

Bab al-Mandeb is one of the world's most important shipping routes. The 20km- (12-mile-)wide waterway lies between Yemen and Djibouti, connecting Europe to Asia. Before fighting resumed, about 12 percent of global trade passed through it. In recent days, the Houthis have grabbed most of Yemen's Red Sea coast, including Mayyun (Perim) Island, which lies in the strait.

"The Houthis seek to move closer to this vital waterway to threaten maritime traffic. Such a move aims to keep the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb under the influence of Iran and use them as leverage against regional and international powers," said Fuad Mussed, a Yemeni analyst and author. "This is a strategy Tehran has been pursuing for years."

This is a serious concern for Saudi Arabia, which has been relying on the Red Sea route to export its oil, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Steep rise in young UK nationals detained for smuggling drugs from Asia
articles.summary: Hundreds of Britons have been detained in Thailand on suspicion of attempting to smuggle cannabis to the UK.
articles.body:
The number of young British nationals arrested abroad after being recruited as drug mules more than quadrupled over three years, according to new government figures.

They showed a steep rise from just over 80 arrests in 2023, to more than 340 in 2025 - with the increase driven by cannabis-related offences linked to Thailand and elsewhere in South East Asia.

People are lured by gangs with the "promise [of] free travel or a quick way to make cash", said Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty, who warned of harsh treatment if detained abroad.

Earlier this year, a BBC investigation found Thailand-based drug gangs were recruiting people to transport large quantities of cannabis in suitcases.

In some instances, people were told they would be carrying suitcases full of clothes, gold or cash. Instead, they contained up to 71kg of cannabis.

Cannabis is a Class B drug in the UK, with penalties of up to five years in prison for possession and up to 14 years for supply and production, as well as unlimited fines.

The Foreign Office said more than 200 British nationals have been detained on suspicion of smuggling cannabis from Thailand, a popular tourist destination. Since 2024, around 60% of them have been aged between 16 and 20.

Young people are commonly recruited on social media and are often incentivised to carry luggage for gangs without knowing its contents.

According to research commissioned by the Foreign Office, a third of young Britons surveyed did not consider travelling with luggage packed by someone else to be a risk.

Penalties for smuggling overseas include prison sentences, fines, corporal punishment such as whipping, or in some cases, the death penalty.

Doughty said "no holiday, payment or opportunity is worth risking your freedom, your future or your life".

He continued: "Detainees are warning about the dire living conditions they now face decades of in prison or, in some countries, the possibility of the death penalty."

One Briton detained abroad described a "sense of mourning for the life" they previously had, while another said: "It's your freedom you're risking, and once it's gone, it's not easy to get back."

Smuggling from Malaysia, Laos and Cambodia was also cited by the UK government as common smuggling sources, as it launched a campaign to deter young British nationals from transporting illicit cargo.

In July, the National Crime Agency (NCA) said British "mules" caught smuggling cannabis from Thailand would face prison, and would have to pay Thai Customs 30,000 Baht (£680) per kilogram to leave the country.

So far in 2026 there have been more than 160 cases of British nationals arrested overseas for drug smuggling offences, the Foreign Office said.

In 2024, police seized £13.8m worth of cannabis smuggled from Thailand at Birmingham Airport. Eight of the 11 people convicted for their involvement last month were in their twenties.

articles.title: Phoenix turned shipping containers into 40 private transitional homes for homeless seniors; each 160-sq-ft unit has a bathroom, and 56 permanent apartments are planned next
articles.summary: US News: The city of Phoenix has decided to tackle homelessness with a new method. What was once designed to carry goods across oceans is now serving a very di.
articles.body: The city of Phoenix has decided to tackle homelessness with a new method. What was once designed to carry goods across oceans is now serving a very different purpose in Phoenix, Arizona: giving older people experiencing homelessness a private place to sleep, shower and begin rebuilding their lives.The city recently opened a new project offering a transitional housing community made from shipping containers for older adults facing homelessness. On Wednesday, city officials gathered for the opening of Senior Bridge, which provides 40 individual transitional housing units for adults aged 55 and older who are experiencing homelessness and need light-touch support as they work toward permanent housing. It is located at 28th and Van Buren streets. The collaboration is between the City of Phoenix and the Arizona Department of Housing and is operated by Mercy House.Each unit measures just 160 square feet, but it is designed to function as a self-contained living space. Residents have a bed, sink, toilet, shower, microwave and small refrigerator. The project is operated by Mercy House in partnership with the City of Phoenix and the Arizona Department of Housing. The City of Phoenix contributed $750,000 toward the 40-unit first phase. It is also investing another $9.6 million in the project's second phase, which is planned to provide 56 affordable housing units.From shipping containers to private roomsAt first glance, the Senior Bridge units look more like an industrial experiment than conventional housing. The containers have been modified into compact private rooms, with basic amenities built into the limited space. Unlike a traditional emergency shelter, however, residents have their own individual units and private bathrooms.The first phase opened on March 25, 2026, at 28th and Van Buren streets in Phoenix. The 40 units are intended for people aged 55 and older who are experiencing homelessness and are capable of living independently with limited support. The small footprint is part of what makes the project distinctive. Each 160-square-foot unit is roughly comparable in floor area to a small bedroom plus bathroom, yet it contains the essentials needed for someone to live there temporarily.The entire complex is designed to run on solar power, with lithium battery storage. According to Mercy House chief program officer Timothy Huynh, the site can operate completely off the electrical grid. That feature could be particularly relevant in Phoenix, where extremely hot summers can place enormous demands on electricity infrastructure. The solar-and-battery system also gives the development an element of resilience while reducing its dependence on conventional grid power.Mercy House officials told Axios that there is no fixed maximum length of stay, but residents are ideally expected to move on to permanent housing within about 90 days. Each resident is paired with a case manager who can help connect them with healthcare, nutrition assistance and community services. Those services are important because the project is designed as a bridge rather than simply a place to sleep.People experiencing homelessness are not a single group, and older adults can face particular challenges when trying to move from the street or a shelter into stable housing. Senior Bridge specifically targets adults 55 and older who need a safe and stable place while they work toward permanent accommodation. The city describes the development as transitional housing for people who need relatively light support rather than intensive residential care. The idea is to give residents enough stability to address the barriers that may have contributed to their homelessness while simultaneously working toward their next housing option.What comes next?The 40 shipping-container units are only the first stage of the Senior Bridge project. The second phase is planned to add 56 permanent supportive apartments, significantly larger than the temporary units. The apartments are expected to be around 750 square feet each, according to Axios, and residents will pay affordable rent while not having to pay power bills. Construction of the container-based apartments was underway, with residents expected to begin moving in around early December.That means the development is being designed to provide a pathway between temporary and longer-term housing rather than treating transitional accommodation as the final solution.The city has also highlighted Senior Bridge as part of its broader response to homelessness. Its Office of Homeless Solutions lists the project as providing 40 units of transitional housing for seniors aged 55 and older, with a future phase of permanent supportive housing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
